country.comment: Single-country urban water case study of Ghana (citing urban data and examples from Accra, Kumasi, Sekondi-Takoradi, Cape Coast, and Tamale), with brief secondary references to Cote d'Ivoire and Cameroon.

effect_estimate.comment: Synthesizes secondary descriptive statistics from NDPC (2010), AVRL (2010), World Bank (2010), Kuma et al. (2010), Abraham et al. (2007), Ghana Statistical Service (2007), UNDP (2006, 2007), and Nyarko et al. (2006); no primary regression estimates, confidence intervals, p-values, or survey sample Ns are reported in the paper.
effect_estimate.value: No primary econometric/statistical effect estimate reported (secondary synthesis). While urban improved water coverage rose from 86% to 93% (1990-2008) and private operator AVRL's billed water rose from 100 to 107 million m3 (2006-2008; revenue rising from GHS 54 million [US$27.69 million] in 2005 to >GHS 100 million [US$51.28 million] in 2008), market-oriented restructuring and fragmented PURC regulation failed to secure 'deep access': in Accra, 46% of AVRL-connected households received water 'only sometimes' or 'rarely' and 5% 'never' had sufficient water; Kumasi supply fell from 66 L/person/day (1996) to 39 L/person/day vs the 94 L/day benchmark; secondary tanker prices reached ~12 times official PURC tariffs (with poor households spending 9%-15% of income on water); and GWCL piped connections were skewed toward higher earners (Accra: 57% for <GHS 100/month vs >70% for GHS 501-1,000 and 83% for GHS 1,001-2,000; urban Ghana: 18.5% inside pipe in lowest quintile vs 43% in highest quintile).
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 3, Introduction; PDF pp. 6-8, Access to water; PDF p. 9, Lessons, implications, and concluding remarks

mechanism_certainty.comment: Design ceiling under Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework is 2. Rated 1 (documented association) because the paper conducts no primary direct empirical observation of administrative or regulatory processes, instead synthesizing descriptive secondary statistics from the market-restructuring/AVRL management-contract period and secondary institutional accounts (e.g., Bohman 2010; Robertson 2011) linking user fees, private management contracting, and PURC's lack of a formal relationship and data sharing with AVRL to persistent deficits in reliability, affordability, quality, and equitable piped access.

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines introduction of user fees, subsidy removal, official PURC tariff policy, and high secondary market pricing (BURDEN: fees); decoupling of urban/rural agencies and regulatory disconnect/lack of formal relationship and data sharing between regulator PURC, asset owner GWCL, and private operator AVRL under the Public Utilities Regulatory Commission Act, Act 538 of 1997 (ENFORCEMENT, institutional_fragmentation); and civil-society contestation, community self-help, and proposed 'public-people partnerships' (participation).
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF p. 4, Modern history of urban water provision in Ghana; PDF pp. 5-6; PDF p. 7, Access to water; PDF pp. 9-10, Lessons, implications, and concluding remarks

outcome_flags.comment: Contrasts 'wide' coverage (service_coverage, water_access) with 'deep' dimensions including tap/groundwater/tanker contamination (service_quality), intermittent and irregular water flow under AVRL (service_reliability, service_continuity), declining per-capita litres/day and production-consumption deficits (service_quantity), high tanker prices and household income shares spent on water (affordability), and income disparities in household GWCL piped connections (formal_connection).

sample_size.comment: No primary empirical sample is collected or reported by the author; the article is an institutional-historical and political-economy case study synthesizing secondary studies, official reports/surveys (e.g., World Bank 2010, Ghana Statistical Service 2007, UNDP 2006/2007, NDPC 2010), and statutory/regulatory documents.

study_design.comment: Framed by the author as a case study of urban water management in Ghana (1957-2011), combining historical-institutional analysis of public-private restructuring, statutory/regulatory critique of the Public Utilities Regulatory Commission Act (Act 538, 1997), and synthesis of secondary quantitative surveys and scientific water-quality studies; no primary data collection or systematic review protocol is reported.
study_design.value: Single-country institutional-historical and political-economy case study using secondary empirical data, official reports, and statutory/regulatory analysis
